evals.prompt:
Use ONLY the control list below to judge overlap with the existing corpus — not the live risk-map/yaml/controls.yaml, which changes over time (per ADR-033 Amendment 2026-07-30, this is a pinned eval fixture, not corpus content):

- controlToolCredentialLifecycleManagement — issue, rotate, and revoke credentials granted to agent tool integrations, scoping credential lifetime to the session or task that requested them so a credential does not remain valid after the agent's task concludes.
- controlAgentActionAuthorizationGating — require an explicit authorization decision (human or policy engine) before an agent executes a high-consequence action.
- controlModelOutputProvenanceLabeling — attach provenance metadata to model-generated output so downstream consumers can distinguish it from human-authored content.
- controlDataRetentionScheduling — enforce a defined retention and deletion schedule for stored data, including agent-collected data.
- controlThirdPartyToolVettingProcess — vet and approve third-party tools before they are made available for agent invocation.
- controlAgentReasoningTraceLogging — capture the agent's reasoning trace (not just the actions taken) for later audit and incident reconstruction.

Stress-test this draft control:

Title: Agent Tool Invocation Allowlisting
Description: Restrict an agent to invoking only tools whose identity is cryptographically verified against an explicit, pre-registered allowlist, denying by default any call to a tool that is absent from the list or whose signature does not match its registered entry. The allowlist and its signing trust root are stored in an admin-controlled store separate from the tool registry itself, so compromising the registry alone cannot forge a passing signature. Identity here means a signed manifest or publisher-attested identifier, not a display name or free-text description — a lookalike name, a typosquatted tool, or a tampered registry entry fails the signature check even if its name matches an allowlisted entry. This bounds which tools an agent can reach at all; it does not evaluate the legitimacy of a specific invocation of an already-allowlisted tool — that is the concern of per-action authorization controls, not this one.
Personas: personaAgenticProvider, personaApplicationDeveloper
Components: componentTools, componentOrchestrationInputHandling
Risks: riskToolSourceProvenance, riskToolRegistryTampering, riskRogueActions
Mappings: nist-ai-rmf: [MEASURE-2.7@1.0]
Counterfactuals: considered blocklisting known-bad tools instead; rejected because default-allow leaves any newly added malicious tool unblocked until discovered. Considered folding this into controlAgentActionAuthorizationGating (fixture); rejected because that control governs a human/policy-engine authorization decision for a specific high-consequence action at the moment it's attempted, while this control is a static, coarser-grained membership check on tool identity performed before any action-level decision is even reached — a tool that fails this gate never gets to the point where an authorization decision would be evaluated. Considered folding this into controlThirdPartyToolVettingProcess (fixture); rejected because vetting is a one-time, pre-availability approval process applied when a tool is onboarded, while this control is an ongoing, per-invocation runtime signature check applied on every call attempt, independent of whether the tool was vetted at onboarding. Considered listing only riskToolSourceProvenance and riskRogueActions; added riskToolRegistryTampering because the signature check is, on its own mechanism, exactly the runtime integrity monitoring against a known-good baseline that risk's text calls for — the check does not depend on whether the tool was ever vetted, so it also defends the post-vetting-compromise case that risk specifically describes. riskToolSourceProvenance is kept as the lead risk (its text names the tool shadowing/typosquatting/schema poisoning attack patterns this mechanism is built against), riskToolRegistryTampering as a second, equally-direct risk, and riskRogueActions as the downstream/cascading risk per riskToolSourceProvenance's own "typically manifests as riskRogueActions" language. NIST AI RMF MEASURE-2.7 chosen following the corpus precedent of controlComponentIdentityProvenance, an identity/integrity-verification control mapped to the same subcategory for the same reason (runtime verification of an invocation-time identity claim) — not the mapping-selection skill's least-privilege/permission-scoping worked example, which is a different control shape than this one. componentOrchestrationInputHandling chosen over componentTools alone because its edge (to: componentTools) places it as the actual dispatch gate between a tool-call decision and the external tool, not just the destination the call lands on.
evals.expected_output: Applies the lenses against the fixture (for control overlap) and the real risks.yaml/controls.yaml/components.yaml/personas.yaml (for risk-linkage, mapping-precedent, and scope precision) and finds the control's premise sound — the enforcement point is real, the mechanism is well-grounded, the three risks are each individually defensible, and the counterfactuals against the two closest fixture entries are genuine, not strawmen — but surfaces specific, well-evidenced gaps in how precisely the draft's efficacy claims are scoped (e.g. whether the mechanism defends a compromised-publisher-key case as well as a registry-tampering case, whether the persona list matches the scope of the precedent it cites, whether cryptographic signing is stated as the objective or as an example). This is a well-formed but underspecified draft, not a duplicate and not a broken premise: verdict NEEDS-WORK, not RETHINK, and not SOUND.
expectations: Uses only the fixture list provided in the prompt, not the live controls.yaml, to judge control-overlap/duplication (D7a) — but may and should still check the real risks.yaml/controls.yaml/components.yaml/personas.yaml for risk-linkage, mapping-precedent, and scope precision, since those are different corpus files from the one being fixture-pinned

Overall verdict is NEEDS-WORK — not SOUND (the draft is genuinely underspecified on at least one load-bearing point), and not RETHINK (the premise itself — a pre-invocation tool-identity gate — is not a duplicate of any fixture entry and is not fundamentally broken)

Every finding raised quotes specific draft text and cites specific, real corpus evidence (a risk's own wording, a real sibling control's mapping or persona list, a real component edge) — none are vague, stylistic-only, or unsupported by a citation

Confirms (does not dispute) that the two counterfactuals against the closest fixture entries (controlAgentActionAuthorizationGating, controlThirdPartyToolVettingProcess) are genuine, non-strawman distinctions — this part of the draft is not itself a finding

Does not collapse into a pure altitude-check T1-T6 listing — findings are framed through the critic's own lenses (efficacy, altitude honesty, generalization, counterfactual quality) with its own tag taxonomy (SUPPORTED/WEAK/UNSUPPORTED/MISAPPLIED-ANALOGY/OVERREACH), not restated as raw altitude-check output

evals.prompt:
Stress-test this draft control:

Title: Agent Prompt Injection Resilience
Description: Addresses prompt injection by ensuring the agent is aware that untrusted content may contain injected instructions.
Risks: riskPromptInjection
evals.expected_output: Tags the efficacy claim UNSUPPORTED (or WEAK): 'awareness' is not a mechanism that reduces the risk, only a naming of it, and would not hold against a determined adversary. Overall verdict NEEDS-WORK or RETHINK — the draft's sparseness (no persona, no locus) may also surface a legitimate T6 novelty/duplicate question against existing risk-scoped controls, which would justify escalating to RETHINK; either verdict is acceptable as long as it isn't SOUND.
expectations: Tags an efficacy finding UNSUPPORTED or WEAK on the claim that the control addresses prompt injection through the agent being 'aware' of injected instructions
Quotes the specific draft text ('ensuring the agent is aware that untrusted content may contain injected instructions') as the challenged claim
Explains that naming or being aware of a risk is not the same as reducing it, especially against a determined adversary
Overall verdict is NEEDS-WORK or RETHINK, not SOUND

evals.prompt:
Stress-test this draft control:

Title: Agent Action Policy Enforcement Point
Description: Implements a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) that intercepts every agent tool call and enforces access decisions using attribute-based access control (ABAC).

The draft does not describe where or how the access decision itself is made, and does not define any attributes or policies the ABAC model would evaluate against.
evals.expected_output: Tags a MISAPPLIED-ANALOGY finding: the draft invokes the PEP/ABAC reference architecture but omits the Policy Decision Point and the attribute/policy definitions that make the model coherent — an enforcement point with no decision point enforces nothing meaningful. Overall verdict NEEDS-WORK.
expectations: Tags a MISAPPLIED-ANALOGY finding on the PEP/ABAC framing
Identifies specifically what is missing for the analogy to be coherent: the Policy Decision Point (PDP) and the attribute/policy definitions ABAC requires
Quotes the draft's PEP/ABAC language as the specific text under challenge
Overall verdict is NEEDS-WORK, not SOUND, since a half-applied reference architecture is treated as a load-bearing weakness

evals.prompt:
This draft control maps to mitre-atlas: [AML.M9999@5.0.1] (correctly a mitigation, not a technique, for a control). I think that identifier might be stale or made up — can you challenge it?

Title: Agent Privileged Action Confirmation
Description: Require explicit confirmation before an agent executes a privileged or irreversible action.
Mappings: mitre-atlas: [AML.M9999@5.0.1]
evals.expected_output: Treats the identifier's currency as something to verify, not assert from memory, and reports concrete evidence for the verdict rather than a bare assertion that it 'looks wrong.' Since MITRE ATLAS never qualifies for the closed-and-unversioned live-verify exemption, the evidence must show genuine live-verification (an actual external/web check) — a corpus-range comparison alone is not sufficient. The critic states it invoked the audit-framework-mappings skill in candidate mode (entity type: control) and tags this as a finding (e.g. UNSUPPORTED) rather than silently correcting the mapping itself.
expectations: Does not assert the identifier's validity or invalidity as a bare claim — shows evidence of genuine live-verification (an actual external/web check attempted or performed), not merely a local corpus-range heuristic; MITRE ATLAS never qualifies for the closed-and-unversioned live-verify exemption, so a comparison against corpus-observed id ranges alone is not sufficient evidence
States which audit-framework-mappings skill mode it used — candidate mode, since this draft control has no row in controls.yaml — and the entity type (control)
Concludes AML.M9999 is not a real/current identifier (fabricated or far outside the real id range), not merely 'possibly stale'
Does not silently accept or correct the mapping itself — includes it as an explicit finding (e.g. tagged UNSUPPORTED) in the output
The overall verdict is not SOUND while this finding stands unresolved

evals.prompt: Stress-test this proposed addition to the real, existing corpus control controlInputValidationAndSanitization (risk-map/yaml/controls.yaml — not a fixture): a PR proposes adding a fifth mitre-atlas mapping, AML.M0021@5.0.1, on the grounds that generative-AI guideline/guardrail-style prompt safety controls are a natural extension of this control's existing adversarial-query-blocking scope. evals.expected_output: Looks up controlInputValidationAndSanitization in the real, live controls.yaml and finds its current mitre-atlas mappings are AML.M0010@5.0.1, AML.M0015@5.0.1, AML.M0020@5.0.1, AML.M0024@5.0.1 — 4 total, not just the single proposed value. Confirms AML.M0021@5.0.1 (Generative AI Guidelines) is itself a real, current, correctly-classified mitigation (mitigation, not technique) genuinely relevant to the control's purpose — the candidate value's own currency and class are not the problem. But because the control already carries 4 mitre-atlas mappings, adding a fifth would push the framework's count to 5, exceeding the soft cap of 4 per risk-map/docs/contributing/framework-mappings-style-guide.md's selectivity rule — a finding only reachable by pulling the complete existing set from the corpus rather than evaluating the proposed value in isolation. States it used single-entity mode (entity type: control) since this is an existing corpus control, not a new draft. The style guide itself frames the soft cap as a prompt to re-examine, not a validation error, so the response may land on either NEEDS-WORK or a SOUND-with-explicit-caveat verdict — what matters is that the overshoot is surfaced as a finding either way, not silently passed over.
expectations: Looks up the real, live risk-map/yaml/controls.yaml entry for controlInputValidationAndSanitization rather than evaluating the proposed AML.M0021@5.0.1 value in isolation

Names the specific existing mitre-atlas mappings it found on that control (AML.M0010@5.0.1, AML.M0015@5.0.1, AML.M0020@5.0.1, AML.M0024@5.0.1 — 4 total) as evidence the complete per-framework set was pulled, not just the single challenged value

Concludes that adding this fifth value would push the framework's mapping count on this control to 5, exceeding the soft cap of 4, and explicitly surfaces this as a finding rather than silently ignoring it, citing risk-map/docs/contributing/framework-mappings-style-guide.md (not a skill) as the source of the soft-cap rule
